cues.text: Seven Figures, Carved for Devotion
The Benedictine monastery of Sant Joan de les Abadesses , in the Catalan Pyrenees, had already stood for over three centuries.
In 1251, a layman named Dolcet and a canon of the monastery, Ripoll Tarascó, commissioned a wooden sculptural group of the Descent from the Cross .
It comprised seven polychrome figures depicting the moment Christ's body was taken down for burial, and was to be installed in the church's central apse.
It was consecrated that same year with relics sealed inside a small reliquary compartment built into the head of the figure of the crucified Christ.
A Reliquary Hidden in Plain Sight
What exactly had been placed inside that hidden compartment went unrecorded, or at least unremembered, as the generations passed.
The sculpture itself, however, remained an object of steady local devotion, installed in the very apse for which it had been carved.
It was never removed or replaced as fashions in religious art changed around it.
The Host Discovered

In 1426, tradition holds, the small reliquary in the head of the Christ figure was opened, and those present found inside a consecrated Host — intact, apparently untouched by the nearly two centuries since the sculpture's original consecration.
The discovery transformed a locally admired work of religious art into a Eucharistic relic in its own right.
The Most Holy Mystery
From that discovery, the sculpture took on the name it has carried ever since: the Santíssim Misteri , the Most Holy Mystery.
Devotion to it grew into one of Catalonia's most enduring local Eucharistic traditions.

Uniquely among surviving medieval sculptural groups of its kind, the Descent remains installed in the same chapel built for it in the thirteenth century—a continuity of place historians attribute directly to the depth and consistency of that devotion.
Legacy
The Host itself disappeared during the anticlerical violence of the Spanish Civil War in 1936, alongside so much else of Catholic Spain's sacred art and relics during those same years.
The sculpture that once concealed it survived and remains today in the church of Sant Joan de les Abadesses.
Its carved wounds and lowered arms still draw the same quiet, kneeling attention that first led a layman and a canon to commission it nearly eight centuries ago.
